newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Great White Shark protected off east Australia.
newsitem.headline: Great White Shark protected off east Australia.

text.p: The Great White Shark, demonised in films like Jaws, on Tuesday became a protected species off Australia's east coast, sparking calls for a worldwide ban on killing white pointers to protect their dwindling numbers.

"Years of irrational hatred and indiscriminate hunting and destruction have taken taken their toll," said Bob Martin, fisheries minister for New South Wales state, in announcing the protected status for the white shark (Carcharodon carcharias).
"It is time to stop demonising the species and start recognising it as a fine example of top-of-the-chain evolution," Martin said.

Despite its media image as the "White Death" and the fact that it is one of the world's largest sharks, growing to 5.5 metres (18 feet) and weighing 2.5 tonnes, the white shark has not been responsible for most of Australia's shark attacks.
That dubious honour goes to the Whaler shark, says John West, zoologist at Sydney's Taronga Zoo.
In all, 527 shark attacks have been recorded in Australia since European settlement in 1788, 184 of which have been fatal.
The latest fatal attack occurred in 1993 at Byron Bay on the NSW north coast when a scuba diver was savaged by a white pointer after pushing his newlywed wife out of danger.

The protected status for the white pointer in NSW waters, which stretch 1,900 km (1,160 miles) along the Australian east coast and three nautical miles offshore, carries a A$20,000 (US$16,000) fine and/or six months in jail for anyone found killing or possessing a Great White Shark.

The Great White is already protected in the waters off Australia's southern island state of Tasmania and from commercial fishing in South Australia. The southeast Australian state of Victoria also plans to protect the white shark.
The Great White Shark is also protected in the waters off South Africa, the U.S. state of California and the Maldives.

The Australian branch of Humane Society International on Tuesday called on the national Australian government to declare the white shark a protected species in Australia's 200 nautical mile territorial waters and support a global protection order.
Society director Michael Kennedy urged Australia to seek international protection under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES).
CITES meets in Harare, Zimbabwe, next June to consider nominations for protection under the convention and nominations must be lodged by January 10.

"CITES will not meet for another four years and that will be too late. We need a global ban on the Great White Shark now -- it has already been classified as a species vulnerable to extinction," Kennedy told Reuters.
Kennedy said the society understood U.S. authorities were keen to co-sponsor a CITES nomination with Australia.

Twenty years after U.S. filmmaker Steven Spielberg terrified the world out of the water with his Hollywood movie Jaws, and 400 million years since fish began gliding through the oceans, the shark has turned from predator to prey.
Marine biologists estimate some 100 million sharks are killed by humans each year as demand for shark products has never been greater.

Dried shark cartilage is used in cancer treatments and to make articial skin for burns victims, shark liver is used in cosmetics, shark gall bladder is used in acne treatments, Great White Shark teeth are used for jewellery, shark "flake" flesh is used in fish and chip shops and shark fin is an Asian delicacy.
Unlike other fish which spawn thousands of eggs at a time, sharks produce only a few dozen, leaving them unable to sustain heavy fishing. Great Whites also takes 20 years to mature.

Great Whites usually live in colder, temperate waters off southern Australia, but travel north along the NSW coast to warmer waters to breed. "We want to allow them to keep going through to their breeding grounds," Martin said.

However, Martin said shark netting of 50 beaches to protect swimmers along the NSW coast would continue. "As magnificent as these shark species are, I'm afraid we have a higher duty to protect the beach going public," he said.
Marine conservationists have called for an end to shark nets, claiming the nets are responsible for the deaths of scores of harmless sharks such as Hammerhead and toothless Wobbegongs.
The number of dangerous sharks caught each year, such as Bronze Whaler and Tiger Shark, have dropped to an average of 10. Only a few white sharks are caught in nets each year.
In fact, only five of the world's known 365 species of sharks are regarded as dangerous to humans.
